item.title: Eternal Unveils Privacy-Focused AI Platform Dark, Eyes Global Launch In 2026
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Zomato and Blinkit parent Eternal has unveiled Dark, a privacy-focused AI platform that founder Deepinder Goyal hopes to launch globally…
item.content:encoded:
Zomato and Blinkit parent Eternal has unveiled Dark, a privacy-focused AI platform that founder Deepinder Goyal hopes to launch globally within 2026.

In Eternal’s Q2 FY27 shareholder letter, Goyal said the platform is aimed at power users, including founders, researchers, scientists, enterprises, and governments, who want to keep their conversations and research private.

Dark has been in internal use for a few months, he said, adding that its privacy features had encouraged him to share more information and explore questions he would hesitate to ask other AI assistants.

The platform uses fine-tuned frontier open-weight models running on Eternal’s own infrastructure. Unlike building a model from scratch, this approach involves adapting existing models whose trained parameters are available for developers to use and modify.

According to Goyal, Dark uses end-to-end encryption, alongside an encrypted memory management layer controlled by users, to retain context across sessions.

“We cannot read your conversations, even if we are forced to,” he said.

He positioned Dark around concerns that users’ interactions with mainstream AI assistants could be retained or accessed by others, discouraging them from sharing sensitive information.

He argued that disabling the use of conversations for model training does not, by itself, address questions around data retention, legal holds, human reviews, or third-party logging.

Eternal’s AI Ambitions

Goyal said concerns around data retention, human reviews, legal holds and third-party logging on mainstream AI platforms could limit the extent to which people use AI for sensitive or commercially valuable work.

He argued that founders, researchers and scientists may hesitate to share breakthrough ideas with AI tools over fears that their information could be accessed by others. Similarly, individuals may avoid asking AI assistants sensitive questions about their health, finances or relationships because of privacy concerns.

Dark aims to address these concerns by combining data privacy with what Eternal describes as high-quality AI responses. The company said it has fine-tuned its models to deliver answers that prioritise truth over user approval, adding that benchmark results would be disclosed later.

Goyal also highlighted the potential risks associated with AI companies retaining user conversations, questioning whether such data could eventually be used to influence consumer behaviour or shape users’ beliefs. 

However, not many details about the platform are available yet. “Dark will launch globally, hopefully within 2026,” Goyal said in the letter. 

With Dark, Eternal has doubled down on its strategy to commercialise AI capabilities developed for its own operations. In February last year, it launched AI-native customer support platform Nugget after building it as an internal tool over three years to handle millions of customer support interactions per month across Zomato, Blinkit and Hyperpure. 

Nugget offers businesses conversational chatbots and co-pilots, alongside voice AI, image classification and workflow automation to businesses. 

These disclosures came as Eternal reported a 92% surge in its net profit to ₹125 Cr in the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27), from ₹65 Cr in the previous year’s quarter. On a sequential basis, profit rose 36% from ₹92 Cr.

Operating revenue for the quarter zoomed 78% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,138 Cr. Including other income of ₹351 Cr, total income stood at ₹24,489 Cr.

District Faces Higher Risk From Agentic Commerce

Apart from outlining its own AI ambitions, Eternal also raised concerns about the impact of agentic commerce on its group companies. Notably, it said its going-out vertical District faces the highest potential disruption from AI agents as they could bypass the platform to discover restaurants, book tables and purchase event tickets, reducing the platform’s role as an intermediary.

Goyal classified District as being in the medium-to-high risk zone, warning that AI agents could weaken content-led competitive advantages, including reviews, ratings and curated listings, by synthesising information from across the internet. However, he believes competition could increasingly favour platforms with stronger execution capabilities.

Meanwhile, he said that Zomato and Blinkit are relatively insulated from agentic commerce because their businesses rely on complex fulfillment infrastructure rather than discovery alone.

According to consumer surveys cited by Goyal, over 65% of Zomato app openings are exploratory, with users browsing an average of 12 menus and more than 100 food images before ordering. He argued that food discovery is an enjoyable activity that conversational AI may not easily replace.

While repeat orders and restocking could shift to AI agents, Eternal said reordered carts account for only a low-single-digit share of activity on both Zomato and Blinkit. It also believes in-app AI assistants could cater to these use cases.

More importantly, food delivery and quick commerce require real-time coordination between restaurants, delivery partners, inventory systems, pickers and dispatch operations. He argued that agents could initiate transactions, but the platforms managing fulfillment would remain responsible for delivering orders and resolving issues. 

This comes as consumer companies are increasingly exploring agent-led shopping and payments. In February 2026, Razorpay and NPCI demonstrated agentic payments through Anthropic’s Claude, enabling users in a pilot to order food and groceries from platforms including Zomato, Swiggy and Zepto within AI conversations.

Meanwhile, Meesho has developed Vaani, a voice-first, multi-agent commerce system designed to help users discover and compare products conversationally.

item.title: Mygate To Merge With Adtech Startup AdOnMo, Eternal To Hold 4.4% Stake
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Community management startup Mygate and adtech startup AdOnMo are set to merge, the startups said in a joint statement today. …
item.content:encoded:
Community management startup Mygate and adtech startup AdOnMo are set to merge, the startups said in a joint statement today. 

The statement came after Eternal’s board approved a deal to transfer its entire shareholding in the digital advertising platform to Mygate, as part of a proposed merger between the two startups.

Post the merger, which is subject to customary conditions precedent and necessary statutory approvals, Eternal will own around 4.4% of the merged Mygate entity on a fully diluted basis, with its stake currently valued at ₹156 Cr. 

Eternal had invested ₹112 Cr in AdOnMo in January 2022, making the current value of its proposed holding 39.3% higher than its original investment. The transaction involves a share exchange rather than a cash payout.

Mygate’s FY26 turnover rose 33% to ₹229 Cr from ₹171 Cr in FY25, as per Eternal. Speaking with Inc42 earlier this year, Mygate CEO Abhishek Kumar claimed that the startup closed FY26 with a top line of ₹232 Cr with an EBITDA margin of 10-12%.

As per Eternal’s disclosures, the deal is expected to fructify by December 5. However, the companies refrained from commenting on the timeline.

Post the merger, AdOnMo’s cofounders, Sandeep Bommireddi and Sravanth Gajula, will join Mygate’s board as cofounders to build and scale the combined company. 

Speaking to Inc42, AdOnMo cofounder Sravanth Gajula said merger discussions began about a year ago, with both startups exploring ways to combine their presence across residential communities and other high-engagement environments. The talks gained momentum over the past six months as the teams explored potential synergies.

The combined entity will bring together Mygate’s community platform, which is used by 60 Lakh households across 30,000 residential communities and AdOnMo’s network of more than 55,000 connected digital screens across 27 cities.

The combined entity can now not only offer resident welfare associations (RWAs) the best-in-class community management platform but also a passive, non-intrusive way to monetise common areas such as lobbies, gates, clubhouses and elevators.

“Coming together with AdOnMo gives us a powerful new way to enhance security & community living. Communities gain an integrated digital screen infrastructure to communicate critical updates and information effortlessly with residents—all while we continue to uphold the trust and privacy our community residents expect from us,” Mygate CEO and cofounder Abhishek Kumar said.

The merger comes shortly after a fresh fund raise for Mygate, which saw it raise ₹225 Cr from Dharana Capital. The startup is currently looking to expand its footprint across gated communities and strengthen its integrated platform.

Important to highlight that Mygate has also seen leadership changes over the past few years. In 2024, cofounder Vijay Arisetty transitioned from his advisory role to focus on Aurm. In June 2025, Mygate elevated its chief business officer, Rohit Jindal, to cofounder.

item.title: Eternal’s Q2 Profit Surges 92% YoY to ₹125 Cr
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Eternal, the parent company of Blinkit and Zomato, reported a consolidated net profit of ₹125 Cr for the second quarter…
item.content:encoded:
Eternal, the parent company of Blinkit and Zomato, reported a consolidated net profit of ₹125 Cr for the second quarter of FY27, up 92% YoY from ₹65 Cr in the previous year quarter. On a sequential basis, profit surged 36% from ₹92 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Operating revenue for the quarter zoomed 78% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,138 Cr. Including other income of ₹351 Cr, total income stood at ₹24,489 Cr. Eternal’s adjusted revenue increased 76% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,621 Cr. On a like-for-like (LFL) basis, adjusted revenue grew 58% YoY.

The difference reflects Blinkit’s shift towards an inventory-led model, under which revenue includes the full value of goods sold directly to customers rather than only marketplace commissions. The like-for-like calculation excludes the cost of goods sold from Blinkit’s own inventory and Hyperpure’s non-restaurant revenue.

Total expenses for the quarter rose 75% YoY to ₹24,166 Cr, while tax expenses came in at ₹198 Cr. Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA almost tripled YoY, surging 197% to ₹666 Cr.

However, the company’s cash balance at the end of September dipped by ₹1,813 Cr to ₹16,475 Cr.

The decline was driven by seasonal net working capital requirements, including building Blinkit’s inventory ahead of the festive season and quarter-end timing in Zomato’s weekly restaurant settlement cycle that temporarily lowered payables.

Besides, Eternal’s board also approved exchanging its entire stake in adtech startup AdOnMo for shares in Mygate ahead of a proposed merger between the two startups. Eternal will eventually own around 4.4% of the merged entity, with the holding currently valued at ₹156 Cr.

The board also approved transferring the India going-out business housed directly in Eternal to wholly owned subsidiary Zomato Entertainment Pvt Ltd for around ₹130.76 Cr, subject to adjustments, through a slump sale. The business housed in two other subsidiaries will subsequently be consolidated into the same entity to streamline operations.

Here’s how Eternal’s key businesses performed during the quarter:

Blinkit Accelerates Store Expansion

Blinkit remained Eternal’s largest revenue contributor, with operating revenue increasing 94% YoY and 22% QoQ to ₹19,152 Cr. On an LFL basis, revenue grew 84% YoY.

The quick commerce business reported a segment profit of ₹488 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA stood at ₹184 Cr, compared with a ₹156 Cr loss in the year-ago quarter.

Blinkit’s net order value (NOV) rose 79.3% YoY and 22.2% QoQ to ₹20,940 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA margin improved for the sixth consecutive quarter to 0.9% of NOV.

The company added 308 net new stores in Q2 FY27, taking its network to 2,751. Eternal now expects Blinkit to cross 3,500 stores by March 2027, raising its earlier target of 3,000, and reach around 5,000 stores by March 2028.

CFO Akshant Goyal said the accelerated expansion was supported by improving performance in smaller cities and newer categories, with new stores meeting the company’s margin and payback expectations.

Eternal expects Blinkit’s adjusted EBITDA margin to continue improving through the expansion, with profitability gains at mature stores and cities offsetting the initial drag from new outlets. Its mature cities already report adjusted EBITDA margins exceeding 5%, while cities contributing around 70% of NOV are adjusted EBITDA positive.

Although annual NOV growth moderated to around 79% owing to a higher base, management expects growth to pick up as new stores open and scale. Blinkit is tracking ahead of its three-year guidance of 60% NOV compound annual growth, but Eternal said it was too early to revise the target upwards.

Zomato’s Growth Regains Pace

Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal reiterated the company’s long-term expectation of more than 20% annual growth in food delivery, following a recovery over the past two quarters.

Zomato’s food delivery NOV increased 21.5% YoY to ₹11,445 Cr. Operating revenue rose 37% YoY to ₹3,396 Cr.

Adjusted EBITDA increased 25% YoY to ₹627 Cr, although its margin declined marginally to 5.5% of NOV. Average monthly transacting customers grew 16% YoY to 28 Mn. 

Goyal attributed part of the previous year’s slowdown to some ordering occasions shifting to quick commerce as the segment expanded. That shift now appears to have stabilised, he said.

Recent growth has been driven by more customers ordering food online and placing orders more frequently. A growing share of new users are ordering food online for the first time, including many outside Zomato’s top eight cities.

“There is still a lot of headroom. Restaurant food is a small part of how India eats. As cities grow, incomes rise and more young people live away from home, we think the food delivery market can keep compounding at 20%+ for many years,” Goyal said.

District Retains Breakeven Timeline

District’s NOV increased 58% YoY and 1.3% QoQ to ₹3,259 Cr. Operating revenue grew 61% YoY to ₹304 Cr, although it declined 4% sequentially.

Its segment loss narrowed to ₹55 Cr from ₹61 Cr in the preceding quarter. Adjusted EBITDA loss remained broadly flat QoQ at ₹64 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA margin improved to -2% of NOV from -3.1% a year ago. CFO Goyal said District remained on track to achieve adjusted EBITDA breakeven within the four-to-six-quarter timeline outlined in January 2026.

Annual NOV growth is running above 50%, ahead of the 30%+ compound annual growth assumption built into its FY30 plan. Eternal retained its FY30 targets of ₹28,000 Cr in NOV and ₹1,400 Cr in adjusted EBITDA.

However, management flagged AI agents that transact on consumers’ behalf as a potential longer-term disruption to parts of the business. Eternal said it is building physical infrastructure and operations that could help District deliver a differentiated customer experience. 

Hyperpure Turns EBITDA Positive

Restaurant supplies business Hyperpure reported operating revenue of ₹1,154 Cr, up 13% YoY. On an LFL basis, revenue increased 22.7%.

Its segment profit stood at ₹19 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA turned positive at ₹10 Cr, as against a loss of ₹5 Cr a year ago.

Hyperpure now serves around 85,000 restaurants, up from 62,000 a year ago.

Management said two-hour deliveries, greater adoption of organised procurement, and services such as kitchen setup were supporting growth. Around 25% of its orders are delivered within two hours.

The others segment, which includes Bistro and Nugget, reported revenue of ₹132 Cr, up 39% from ₹95 Cr in the preceding quarter. Its adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to ₹91 Cr from ₹94 Cr sequentially.

Shares of Eternal ended Wednesday’s trading session 2.71% lower at ₹311.75.

Listed NBFC Aye Finance’s net profit for the September quarter surged 151% to ₹86.7 Cr from ₹34.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. On a sequential basis, profit increased 16% from ₹74.5 Cr. 

Operating revenue grew 18% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹514.4 Cr, led by a 29% YoY increase in interest income to ₹479.3 Cr.

Fees and commission income rose 13% YoY to ₹20.5 Cr. The NBFC also recorded a ₹10.1 Cr gain on derecognition of financial instruments measured at amortised cost and ₹4.5 Cr in net gains from fair value changes.

Including other income of ₹12.7 Cr, total income rose 18% YoY to ₹527.1 Cr.

Loan Book Expands 26%

On the operational front, Aye Finance’s assets under management (AUM) rose 26% YoY and 4% QoQ to ₹7,597 Cr. Loan disbursements increased 10% YoY and 15% QoQ to ₹1,403 Cr.

Its active customer base expanded 18% YoY to 6.94 Lakh, with the lender adding 49,150 new borrowers during the quarter.

The expansion was accompanied by an improvement in asset quality. Its gross non-performing assets ratio declined to 4.2% from 4.5% in the June quarter, while the net ratio eased to 1.6% from 1.7%.

Credit costs fell to 3.8% from 5% a year earlier and 4% in the preceding quarter. Its operating expense ratio declined 100 basis points YoY to 8.6%, the lowest in eight quarters.

“We remain firmly on track to deliver our FY27 growth and earnings guidance while absorbing the expected effects of increased cost of borrowing,” MD Sanjay Sharma said.

He added that the company expects its return on equity to rise over subsequent quarters as it increases leverage against the capital raised through its IPO in February this year.

item.title: SBI Flags Exposure Of 3,897 Customer Records On Dark Web
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: State Bank of India (SBI) has flagged the exposure of 3,897 customer records containing personal information on the dark web,…
item.content:encoded:
State Bank of India (SBI) has flagged the exposure of 3,897 customer records containing personal information on the dark web, including mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, and residential addresses.

The public sector lender, in an exchange filing, said its preliminary analysis of around 3.75 Lakh records available on the dark web identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information.

The data also included branch details, customer information file identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan and lead records, according to the bank.

SBI said it received alerts about the suspected exposure on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In).

The disclosure follows claims attributed to a threat actor using the name Siriusim, which cybersecurity account CyberPulse56 shared on X. The actor claimed to possess around 3.75 Lakh rows of SBI-linked data and 2,722 PDF documents, including loan applications, supporting documents, and account-opening forms. Inc42 could not independently verify these claims.

The number of records examined does not establish that 3.75 Lakh customers were affected, with SBI’s preliminary findings identifying 3,897 customer records containing personal information.

SBI Launches Probe Into Data Exposure

SBI said it had activated its cyber incident response and containment protocols and engaged an independent CERT-In-empanelled cybersecurity agency to investigate.

The investigation will seek to establish the authenticity and completeness of the data, identify the source and extent of the exposure, and assess potential risks to customers and the bank.

The lender said its core banking and business functions continued to operate normally, with no material impact on operations, financial performance, or business continuity. It added that remedial and preventive measures were being implemented while the assessment continued.

The incident comes amid growing concerns over AI-driven cybercrime and digital fraud. State-run Punjab National Bank (PNB) has also warned customers about threats such as AI-generated voice clones, deepfakes and phishing attacks.

The SBI incident follows other customer data breaches at Indian financial services companies. In February last year, Angel One disclosed unauthorised access to some of its Amazon Web Services resources after receiving alerts from its dark-web monitoring partner.

Prior to that, personal data belonging to over 3 Cr Star Health customers surfaced for sale online, including names, addresses, PAN details, and medical histories. The insurer reported the breach to CERT-In and the insurance regulator, initiated a forensic investigation, and moved court to restrict access to the leaked information.

item.title: Can India Capitalise On The AI Homecoming?
item.dc:creator: Ankush Das
item.description: For decades, Indian engineers and researchers moved to Silicon Valley, joining global technology companies and contributing to products and research…
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Indian engineers and researchers moved to Silicon Valley, joining global technology companies and contributing to products and research that shaped the industry. Now, the tides are turning. Indian talent with experience at some of the world’s most influential AI labs is making its way back home to build startups and research organisations of its own.

This emerging trend could signal a new wave of reverse brain drain. But what has changed to make India a more credible place to build AI companies for those who have worked at the world’s leading research labs? And why is this happening now? Let’s ponder in this edition of The AI Shift…

A Land Of Opportunities

The shift is being driven by a combination of entrepreneurial ambition and a changing Indian AI ecosystem. Experienced researchers are beginning to see an opportunity to build companies around their own research agendas, while India’s growing startup landscape and emerging AI infrastructure are making that ambition more achievable.

Shyamal Hitesh Anadkat, a former OpenAI researcher who returned to India to build Empirical Machines, a startup focused on accelerating scientific discovery, pointed to this change in an interview with Financial Express. 

He cited growing momentum in the startup ecosystem, the emergence of companies such as Sarvam AI, and a stronger appetite for risk among researchers and founders. The sense that more talent was beginning to rally around India’s AI opportunity had also become an important factor.

Parth Sarthi, cofounder of Chariot, offers another perspective. After completing his masters from Stanford University, Sarthi joined Contextual AI and later Google DeepMind as a research engineer. His work at DeepMind included multimodal reasoning for Gemini Deep Thinking, involving systems that reason across text, numbers and images.

Sarthi had long felt that India needed to develop similar frontier research capabilities. Limited GPU access had previously constrained the research that could be conducted locally. The IndiaAI Mission’s call for proposals to develop indigenous foundation models made the prospect of building in India more tangible. He saw an opportunity to apply his experience to developing advanced AI capabilities in India rather than continuing to build similar systems for Western markets.

Government support is also helping make the proposition more credible. The IndiaAI Mission is expanding access to compute, supporting indigenous foundation models and providing assistance for AI startups. These initiatives do not eliminate the gap with global AI labs, but they can lower some barriers to experimentation and company formation. Not to forget, AI funding in India grew 235% YoY in Q3 2026, as per Inc42’s latest report.

From Global AI Labs To Indian Startups

Anadkat is among the clearest examples of this shift. After nearly four years at OpenAI, where he led the Applied Evals team, he returned to India in 2026 to build here. The startup aims to use AI to accelerate research involving molecules and materials.

According to Moneycontrol, Empirical Machines is in talks to raise around $15 Mn from Peak XV Partners and Bessemer Venture Partners at a reported valuation of approximately $80 Mn. 

Sarthi’s Chariot is another example of experienced researchers attempting to build frontier AI capabilities from India. The company is developing speech-native foundation models and was among the teams selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop foundational models. His earlier research included RAPTOR, a retrieval technique for language models published at ICLR 2024 and subsequently incorporated into frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. 

The movement also extends to specialised AI infrastructure. Anish Das Sarma, a former Google engineering director, founded Reinforce Labs to build tools that evaluate, red-team and remediate enterprise AI systems. The startup was featured in Peak XV’s Surge cohort, reflecting demand for infrastructure that helps businesses deploy AI more reliably. 

Meanwhile, Sarvam AI has drawn experienced researchers into its effort to build Indian foundation models. These examples represent different forms of talent movement: researchers returning to start companies, experienced technical leaders launching specialised ventures, and global researchers advising Indian startups. They point to a growing willingness to build AI capabilities outside traditional technology hubs.

Are Investors Following The Trend?

For venture capitalists, experience at OpenAI or Google DeepMind can signal familiarity with advanced research, model development and the challenges of taking AI systems into production. It may also help founders recruit specialist talent and establish credibility with customers and investors. But pedigree alone does not establish whether a company can succeed.

Sayantan Sarkar, principal at Stellaris Venture Partners, believes hands-on experience building models at frontier AI labs offers three distinct advantages. Researchers who have worked closely with advanced models can anticipate how the technology is likely to evolve, identify gaps in existing capabilities and spot opportunities to build products for emerging needs.

Their understanding of post-training techniques can also help improve models and develop better products. In addition, their credibility within the AI ecosystem can help attract high-quality researchers and engineers, including those from frontier labs.

Ultimately, Sarkar argues, the advantage is not simply having worked at a leading AI lab, but being able to translate that experience into a differentiated company.

Rahul Mathur, the vice president at DeVC and a pre-seed investor, approaches the question from the founder’s perspective. Mathur believes investors should start by understanding the founder: why they left their previous role, what motivates them to pursue the opportunity, and whether they have the resources and commercial judgement to build a sustainable business.

He also examines the team they have assembled and why its members are willing to leave comfortable or well-paying jobs to join the startup. For AI research ventures, Mathur asks a more fundamental question: what customer-backed research is being conducted, and who will pay for it? He is looking for a “resourceful & commercially sound founder”.

The two perspectives highlight the distinction between technical advantage and investment merit. A researcher may understand how to build an advanced model, anticipate the next wave of capabilities and recruit exceptional talent. But those strengths must translate into a product that solves a real problem and creates a defensible business.

That challenge is particularly acute in AI, where research can take years to translate into a commercial product, while compute, experimentation and specialist talent demand substantial investment. Investors must establish whether a founder can identify a market, prioritise the right research and build a sustainable business around the technology.

A strong research pedigree may open the door, but customer demand, execution and commercial judgement determine whether a company can endure.

For India, the more consequential shift would be one in which experienced researchers build organisations that generate proprietary research, train new talent and sell globally competitive products. The measure of positive reverse brain drain will not be how many researchers leave global labs but how many enduring AI businesses they build from here. 

Top Stories From India & Around The World

  • RapidCanvas Nets $29 Mn: The startup raised $29 Mn in a Series B round led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India to expand go-to-market operations, grow its AI engineering team and strengthen enterprise AI deployment.
  • Confido Health Raises $12.5 Mn: The healthtech startup raised $12.5 Mn in a Series A extension led by Z47 to expand its AI-powered CareOS platform and automate more administrative workflows across healthcare providers.
  • Anthropic Opens Its Models To Safety Evaluators: Anthropic has given researchers at nonprofit METR employee-like access to assess its models, with the independent evaluator expected to publish risk assessment findings as the lab expands external scrutiny of AI safety.
  • Meta’s Algo Under Review: The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has asked Meta to review its content recommendation algorithms, renewing scrutiny of how AI-driven systems rank and distribute content.
  • SaaS Models Under Pressure: Zoho cofounder Sridhar Vembu has sparked a debate on AI economics, warning that rising server prices and token expenditure are pushing up operating costs as software companies grapple with shrinking margins and uncertain returns on AI-driven productivity gains.

The Weekly Buzz: Meta’s Muse Wonder Claims The Frontier

Recently, Meta launched Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, the first frontier-class models from its Superintelligence Labs. The company says the new models reach parity with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s top Claude variants on multistep reasoning, coding, and long-horizon agentic tasks, priced at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

Wonder is positioned as Meta’s largest and most capable model yet, built specifically for agent workflows such as processing insurance claims or complex lease negotiations. It introduces Active Memory and Active Focus features that let the model carry context across conversations and persist through difficult multi-step work. 

A companion open-weight release, Muse Spark Open (816 Bn parameters, nearly 42 Bn active), was optimised with Apple to run efficiently on the Mac Studio. The models power the paid tier of Meta’s Muse personal agent and mark the clearest sign yet that Meta intends to compete head-to-head with the closed frontier labs rather than remaining primarily an open-weights player. 

Early independent benchmarks appear supportive of the parity claims, though full third-party verification is still underway.

With Muse already a consumer hit, the Wonder family gives Meta a credible path to monetise advanced agent capabilities at scale while keeping a strong open-source presence.

Startup In The Spotlight: Coreshield

Founded in 2023 by Chandan Singh Rathore, a former Indian Air Force squadron leader, Bhavya K, an ex-Palo Alto Networks executive, and Rana Amit K N, CoreShield Technologies is building AI-driven security systems to protect critical infrastructure and national assets.

India’s growing geopolitical complexity and rising threats to defence, energy and public infrastructure have made real-time security intelligence increasingly important. However, existing defence and civil protection systems often operate in silos, with cameras, sensors and communication networks functioning independently. This fragmentation can delay threat detection and response during emergencies.

Operating from IIT Delhi’s Research & Innovation Park, CoreShield develops indigenous platforms that integrate video and acoustic analytics, AI-based decision orchestration and secure data-flow monitoring. Its systems bring together intelligence from multiple sources to help defence and infrastructure agencies detect, analyse and respond to threats in seconds.

Designed for both military and civilian applications, the startup aims to improve situational awareness and enable faster, data-driven responses. Its focus on coordinating intelligence across disparate systems differentiates it from solutions that address individual security components in isolation.

With India’s defence tech market projected to grow from $7.6 Bn in 2025 to $19 Bn by 2030, rising defence modernisation and AI adoption could create opportunities for indigenous security platforms such as CoreShield.

Prompt Of The Week

What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work?

item.content:encoded:
Apple India Rolls In Profits

Apple’s India story is no longer just about iPhone sales. In FY26, the smartphone maker’s local unit saw record growth in revenue and profit, while exports and launch of new services further deepened its foothold. So, as component shortages loom, can Apple sustain its India surge?

An Expanding Ecosystem: Apple India’s FY26 performance reflected strong demand across iPhones, Macs, iPads and other products. Revenue from traded goods drove most of the growth, while services such as AppleCare and maintenance contracts further added to the revenue mix.

Here is a quick look at Apple India’s FY26 numbers:

  • Net profit rose 66% YoY to ₹5,311 Cr
  • Operating revenue grew 31.4% YoY to ₹1.04 Lakh Cr
  • Total Expenses also rose 28% YoY to ₹96,224 Cr

The numbers show Apple is building a broader consumer technology business in India rather than relying solely on its flagship smartphone.

The Cost Conundrum: However, Apple’s growth came with a steep price tag. Inventory purchases remained its largest financial drain in FY26, while licensing fees more than doubled to ₹10,374 Cr. Employee costs and marketing expenditure also rose substantially as Apple expanded its operations and strengthened its presence in India.

The India Playbook: All said and done, Apple’s ambitions in India extend beyond sales. The country has become one of its largest production bases outside China, with iPhone exports crossing ₹2 Lakh Cr in FY26. At the same time, it is also expanding its services ecosystem in India. 

The OEM has launched new offerings such as Apple Pay and Fitness+ in the past few months, which are expected to create new revenue streams for the iPhone maker going forward.

The Sombre Outlook: But Apple’s near-term momentum faces pressure due to chip and memory shortages. As such, the company expects supply chain constraints to impact iPhones, Macs and iPads globally, potentially influencing product availability in India.

With demand rising, manufacturing deepening and services entering the ecosystem, here is how Apple fared on the financial front in FY26…

From The Editor’s Desk

Flipkart’s Food Delivery Foray

  • The Walmart-owned ecommerce major plans to roll out its food delivery service, called Eat-in by Minutes, to the general public by October-end this year. The company is said to have expanded its internal pilot in Bengaluru to more than 8,000 employees.
  • Flipkart, which began piloting food delivery internally earlier this year, plans to expand the service to six cities by 2026-end. It has tapped the state-backed ONDC for restaurant onboarding and has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders via its logistics arm Ekart. 
  • Flipkart’s planned launch comes as new rivals take on Zomato and Swiggy. Rapido is offering a zero-commission model to attract eateries to its new foodtech platform Ownly. Swish has also begun piloting food delivery survive in select Bengaluru pincodes.

New Twist In Satcom Saga

  • The Centre is considering developing a hardware device to oversee services offered by Starlink and other overseas satcom operators. All traffic will be routed via the proposed device, which will act as a control layer between users and satellite networks.
  • The government is considering involving public sector R&D units, while keeping participation by select private players open. With this, officials are looking to address risks associated with foreign satellite operators.
  • The plan comes right after Elon Musk accused certain Indian “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s entry into India. The Centre has denied allegations of preferential treatment, maintaining that all applicants are at the same regulatory stage.

IndiaMART Under CCPA Radar

  • The Central Consumer Protection Authority has pulled up seven ecommerce platforms, including IndiaMART and Justdial, for listing and selling unauthorised hazardous explosives such as ammonium nitrate, gun powder, picric acid and PETN.
  • The regulatory action resulted in the delisting of 3,940 sellers and listing entries, including 3.092 at IndiaMART and 206 at Justdial. The CCPA also imposed penalties worth ₹30 Lakh on two platforms namely Dial4Trade and ExportersIndia. 
  • The development comes amid regulatory clampdown on new-age tech consumer brands. Just days ago, CCPA imposed a fine of ₹10 Lakh on Rapido over unfair trade practices. FSSAI has also issued notices to multiple D2C brands and quick commerce players.

Founder FY26 Salary Tracker

  • Twenty-two founders across 15 Indian new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹66.87 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 2.3% from ₹65.34 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Of these, 16 received increases in fixed pay and four saw reductions. 
  • Honasa cofounder Ghazal Alagh saw her fixed remuneration soar 60% YoY to ₹2.4 Cr in FY26, while Delhivery cofounder Sahil Barua followed with a 21.4% YoY jump to ₹3.4 Cr. Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal’s salary fell 34.8% to ₹4.5 Cr.
  • MobiKwik’s Bipin Preet Singh and Upasana Taku were the most paid founders, drawing fixed remuneration of ₹6.3 Cr each in FY26. Lenskart cofounder Peyush Bansal followed at ₹5.7 Cr, down 1.7% from ₹5.8 Cr.

Decoding Burma Burma DRHP

  • Last week, the restaurant chain’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Limited, filed its DRHP with SEBI. The proposed IPO consists of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.79 Cr shares.
  • As per the draft IPO papers, Hunger Pangs has 110 shareholders. Cofounders Ankit Gupta and Chirag Chhajer each hold a 33.35% stake. Its cap table remains heavily concentrated, with top eight stakeholders collectively owning 83.19% in the company.
  • Negen Capital, via its  two funds, holds about 10% stake in the company, while rubber and plastic manufacturing company Bbigplas Poly also owns a 2.72% stake. Venture Catalysts also holds around 1.88% stake in Burma Burma. 

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

How Protein Pantry Is Reimagining Vegetarian Protein

On-the-go snacking and quick meals are becoming the norm for the Indian urban milieu. On this front, choices remain very limited for vegetarians. To solve this, Protein Pantry is building a portfolio of clean-label, high-protein snacks and meals that are designed for quick preparation.

Protein For Daily Needs: Founded in 2025, Protein Pantry sells a range of ready-to-cook frozen foods such as soya chaap, kebabs, cutlets and falafels. The brand claims that its products are baked rather than fried, with no maida, preservatives or palm oil. Each item can be prepared in under three minutes, targeting users who want a protein-rich meal without lengthy cooking.

Healthy Early Traction: Protein Pantry claims to have so far served around 30,000 users and is currently clocking a revenue run rate of ₹7 Cr. It also operates a 10,000+ sq ft facility in Noida and sells its offerings through its website and quick-commerce platforms.

The Road Ahead: Backed by Sharrp Ventures and Indian Silicon Valley Capital, the startup plans to now focus on scaling manufacturing and expanding distribution. Currently operating in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, Protein Pantry plans to expand to more cities in the long-term.

With the Indian frozen food market projected to become a ₹64,364 Cr opportunity by 2034, can Protein Pantry make high-protein food a daily habit for Indians?

Infographic Of The Day

India’s condiment game is getting a glow-up. From pudina chutney and chilli oil to peri-peri mayo and dips, homegrown D2C brands are leaving no stone unturned to grab a pie of the thriving Indian condiment market. So, which startups are adding the extra tadka to our plates…

item.title: Can Hotels Become ixigo’s Fourth Growth Engine?
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Travel tech company ixigo is betting on hotels as its fourth growth engine alongside trains, flights, and buses, as further…
item.content:encoded:
Travel tech company ixigo is betting on hotels as its fourth growth engine alongside trains, flights, and buses, as further market share gains become harder in rail bookings and high airfares and capacity constraints weigh on flights.

The company began reporting hotels as a separate operating segment in Q2 FY27, breaking it out from ‘Others’. The revenue of the hotel segment grew more than sixfold to ₹8.1 Cr, accounting for 2.5% of ixigo’s ₹321 Cr operating revenue in the September quarter.

Its gross transaction value (GTV) reached ₹111.3 Cr, or 2.6X the year-ago figure, making it ixigo’s fastest-growing business line by this measure.

“Hotels took a great leap forward, getting to a critical mark that makes it large enough to start disclosing (separately),” ixigo group CEO Alok Bajpai said during the earnings call.

The segment’s contribution loss widened to ₹1.2 Cr from ₹71 Lakh in Q2 FY26. However, the contribution margin improved to -15% from -55%, as revenue growth outpaced the increase in direct costs.

This loss captures only part of the investment. Much of ixigo’s hotel-related technology, product, and employee spending sits within group costs. Management attributed around ₹10 Cr of the approximately ₹20 Cr increase in group costs, excluding ESOP expenses, to building and scaling hotels.

Its train, flight, and bus businesses generated around ₹126 Cr in contribution profit during the quarter, helping fund the expansion. 

As Inc42’s earlier business model analysis examined, ixigo is reinvesting operating leverage from its established businesses into hotels, AI, and brand building. The latest results show how it is pursuing hotel growth through existing customers and direct property partnerships.

ixigo’s Hotel Blueprint

ixigo is targeting budget and mid-market accommodation, particularly independent hotels, to serve travellers who already book journeys through its platforms but may use offline channels or other services for accommodation.

“The opportunity is particularly compelling in the budget, mid-market, and independent hotels, where online penetration is low, and travellers need greater reliability and peace of mind,” Bajpai said during the earnings call.


Industry estimates cited by the company’s management put India’s hotel market at ₹1.57 Lakh Cr in FY26, projected to reach ₹1.94 Lakh Cr by FY28. Hotel bookings through OTAs are expected to rise from ₹40,200 Cr to ₹57,000 Cr over the same period.

About 60% of hotel room nights in India sell for less than ₹2,000 a night, while independent hotels account for 73% of rooms.

This market overlaps with ixigo’s customer base – 94% of its transactions involve travellers going to or from Tier II and III cities, while more than nine in 10 trips booked are by train or bus.

More than 86% of Q2 hotel bookings came from existing users, which management believes can help it scale without acquiring every hotel customer separately.

ixigo has more than 70,000 hotels on its platforms, including over 12,000 directly contracted properties across around 1,100 towns. Direct partnerships stood at over 10,000 properties across nearly 700 towns in the previous quarter. The company said HELLO, its AI-first hotel partner platform, helped accelerate this expansion.

The Q2 figures also include Brevistay, in which ixigo acquired a 54.66% stake for ₹65.69 Cr. The startup offers rooms for three, six, or 12 hours rather than a full-day stay. ixigo is using the acquisition to expand direct hotel relationships, meaning reported growth includes both organic expansion and Brevistay’s contribution.

While ixigo builds its hotel business, its three established verticals continue to fund the expansion, with differing growth prospects across trains, flights, and buses.

How Are ixigo’s Core Businesses Performing? 

The number of train passenger journeys booked through ixigo rose around 7% YoY to 2.9 Cr in Q2 FY27. Revenue increased 16% to ₹149.1 Cr and contribution profit grew 29% to ₹47.2 Cr.

Management said ixigo’s share of the OTA rail market reached around 64%. With railway capacity growing at an estimated 4-5% annually, further expansion will increasingly depend on new products, monetisation, and cross-selling, alongside booking volumes.


Trains’ share of GTV has fallen from more than half to the low-40% range as other categories expand. Management expects this proportion to decline further, even as the business grows in absolute terms.

Flight GTV increased 37% YoY, but revenue declined 8% to ₹82.7 Cr. The gross take rate fell to 7% from 9.4%, reflecting pressure on monetisation amid higher airfares, capacity constraints, and a changing booking mix. Higher ticket values supported GTV but did not translate into revenue growth.

The festive season provided some support to flight bookings, but management cautioned that the recovery remains uncertain as high airfares and capacity constraints continue to weigh on demand. 

“We hope this improves as the peak of the festive season arrives, though it is too early to call, and this should not be read as guidance,” ixigo said in its earnings release. 

Buses remained a stronger growth channel. Bus GTV increased 32% YoY to ₹752.65 Cr, revenue grew 24% to ₹81.04 Cr, and contribution profit rose 27% to ₹43.14 Cr.

These established businesses provide the earnings and customer reach to support hotels. The challenge is to convert that advantage into sustained growth while managing expansion costs that extend beyond the segment’s reported contribution loss.

item.title: Burma Burma DRHP: A Look At Shareholding Pattern & Key Executives
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Last week, Hunger Pangs Limited, the parent company of restaurant chain Burma Burma, filed its DRHP with SEBI, proposing a…
item.content:encoded:
Last week, Hunger Pangs Limited, the parent company of restaurant chain Burma Burma, filed its DRHP with SEBI, proposing a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.79 Cr shares.

Hunger Pangs has 110 shareholders, including its promoters and public shareholders. Cofounders Ankit Gupta and Chirag Chhajer each hold a 33.35% stake in the company and plan to offload up to 60 Lakh shares each.

Negen Capital, through its Negen Undiscovered Value Fund and Negen Tech Opportunities Angel Fund, holds about 10% stake in the company. The investment firm first invested in Hunger Pangs in November 2022 and doubled down in 2023.

Hunger Pangs’ shareholding remains concentrated, with its top eight shareholders collectively holding 83.19% of the company on a fully diluted basis.

Among the other shareholders, rubber and plastic manufacturing company Bbigplas Poly Private Limited holds a 2.72% stake, while Venture Catalysts owns 1.88%. Individual investors, including Sagun Capital founder Saket Agarwal and Nazara backer Nisarg Ajaykumar Vakharia, each hold about 1% stake in Hunger Pangs.

Burma Burma’s Business

Meanwhile, the fresh issue will help Burma Burma expand its restaurant network, with plans to open 27 company-owned outlets in new Tier I and Tier II cities. The company expects to open 12 outlets in FY28 and another 15 in FY29. The funds will cover civil and interior work, kitchen equipment and other setup costs.

To note, Burma Burma opened its first restaurant in Mumbai in 2014 and specialises in vegetarian Burmese cuisine. As of July 31, 2026, the chain operated 22 restaurants across nine cities, including Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kolkata and Delhi NCR. It also operated a delivery kitchen in Mumbai and three warehouses.

The chain operates in the broader Asian dining segment, competing with restaurant brands such as Mainland China, Mamagoto, Yum Yum Cha and Berco’s.

In March 2026, Burma Burma raised ₹38 Cr at a valuation of ₹500 Cr. The round was led by Negen Capital, with participation from Endurance Capital and Coheron Wealth. The company’s total private funding to date stands at about $11 Mn.

Hunger Pangs’ net loss surged to ₹15.4 Cr in FY26 from ₹50 Lakh in FY25, while operating revenue rose 46.6% YoY to ₹155.5 Cr from ₹106.1 Cr. Dine-in contributed 88.82% of operating revenue in FY26, while delivery accounted for 10.76%.

Who’s At Burma Burma’s Helm?

Board of Directors

Shivakumar Dega

Dega has served as chairman and independent director at Hunger Pangs since July 2026. He has been an operating partner at Advent International since April 2023, according to his LinkedIn profile. He also serves on the boards of companies including iD Fresh, Intellect Design Arena, Leapfrog Strategy Consulting, PGP Glass and Yes Bank.

Ankit Virendra Gupta

Gupta is the cofounder and joint managing director of Hunger Pangs. After completing his management trainee programme at The Taj Mahal Palace in Mumbai, he worked in hotel operations for about two years. Around 2011, he returned to his family business before launching Burma Burma with Chhajer.

Chirag Narendra Chhajer

Chhajer is the cofounder and joint managing director of Hunger Pangs. He graduated in international business from Swinburne University in Melbourne, Australia, in 2008. He subsequently joined Chhajer Synthetics, his family’s textile trading business, before cofounding Burma Burma with Gupta.

Kushal Budhia

Budhia joined Hunger Pangs as an independent director in July 2026. He is the cofounder and group CFO of BetterPlace. Before joining BetterPlace, he spent more than two years at Pepperfry. Over a career spanning 17 years, he has also worked with Barbeque Nation Hospitality, Jupiter Capital and Goldman Sachs.

Lavanya Nalli Ramanathan

Ramanathan joined Hunger Pangs as an independent director in September 2026. She has served as vice chairman of Nalli Silk Sarees since January 2016. Her previous experience includes roles at Myntra and McKinsey. She also serves on the boards of Nalli Silk Sarees and Etnische Fashions.

Pavitra Joshi Singh

Singh joined Hunger Pangs as an independent director in September 2026. She is the chief human resources officer and vice president for PepsiCo India and South Asia, where she has held various leadership roles over a 20-year career.

Key Managerial Personnel And Senior Management

Vishnu Kumar Agarwal

Agarwal joined Burma Burma in 2014 and was elevated to CFO in 2026. His total compensation for FY26 stood at ₹58.5 Lakh.

Abhinav Agarwal

Agarwal was designated company secretary in May 2026 and compliance officer in September 2026. He joined Hunger Pangs in April 2026. Before this, he served as AVP of finance, strategy, legal and investor relations at BRISKPE. He has more than a decade of experience and has also worked with Vayana, theremin.ai and Pantomath Capital Advisors.

Ansab Ajaz Khan

Khan joined Burma Burma in 2014 and was appointed chief of kitchen operations in September 2026. He has previously worked with Mahindra Holidays and Resorts India and Mehul Restaurant and Bar. His total compensation for FY26 was ₹78 Lakh.

Sahil Mohan

Mohan was appointed chief of restaurant operations in September 2026, after 12 years with Burma Burma. He previously worked with Indian Hotels Company Limited and Taj Lands End, Mumbai. His total compensation for FY26 was ₹59.4 Lakh.

Pooja Soman

Soman joined Hunger Pangs in November 2024 and was elevated to chief human resources officer in April 2026. She has more than 17 years of experience in human resources management. Her total compensation for FY26 stood at ₹43.4 Lakh.

item.title: IndiaMART, Justdial Booked By CCPA Over Explosive Products Listings
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has taken regulatory action against seven ecommerce platforms, including IndiaMART and Justdial, over the…
item.content:encoded:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has taken regulatory action against seven ecommerce platforms, including IndiaMART and Justdial, over the listing and sales of unauthorised hazardous explosives.

The material listed on these platforms included ammonium nitrate, gun powder, picric acid and pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN).

Except for ammonium nitrate, all of the aforementioned chemicals are exclusively used in manufacturing explosives.

The regulatory action has resulted in the delisting of 3,940 sellers and listing entries, while the authority has imposed penalties totalling ₹30 Lakh on Dial4Trade and ExportersIndia, the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution said in a statement yesterday.

IndiaMART accounted for the highest number of affected sellers and listings, with 3,092, followed by ExportersIndia with 421, Justdial with 206 and TradeIndia with 166, according to the ministry. Other platforms facing regulatory action include Dial4Trade, Sigma-Aldrich India and Ibuychemikals.

In its statement, the consumer protection body shared that it had issued notices to both Justdial and IndiaMART over the listings. Following the notices, Director General – Investigation investigated the matter and shared their reports with the companies. 

IndiaMART submitted its reply to the investigation report and, subsequently, approached the Delhi High Court challenging the SCN issued by the CCPA. Meanwhile, Justdial has sought adjournments in the matter till now and is yet to respond to the investigation. The next and final hearing in the matter is scheduled to be held on October 23.

 Meanwhile, the CCPA has imposed a penalty of ₹10 Lakh on Dial4Trade for facilitating the sale of ammonium nitrate. ExportersIndia was fined ₹10 Lakh in two separate cases, one involving ammonium nitrate and Pentaerythritol Tetranitrate (PETN), and the other involving picric acid.

The CCPA’s action covers both marketplaces that host third-party sellers and platforms that sell products directly. Sigma-Aldrich Chemicals and Ibuychemikals have told the authority that they sell their own products and do not host third-party sellers. Investigations into TradeIndia, Sigma-Aldrich Chemicals and Ibuychemikals are ongoing.

Dial4Trade challenged the order before the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC), which dismissed its appeal on October 9. The commission held that the listings amounted to misleading advertisements and unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

ExportersIndia has also appealed against the CCPA’s orders before the NCDRC. The appeals are expected to be listed for hearing in the coming period.

Consumers can report listings of explosives on online platforms through the national consumer helpline at 1915.

Under the Explosives Act, 1884, the sale and purchase of these substances require prescribed licences. The CCPA expects platforms to ensure sellers display valid licences issued by the petroleum and explosives safety organisation (PESO) and verify buyers’ identities and licence status before allowing purchases.

“The action reinforces the Government’s commitment to ensuring that digital marketplaces do not facilitate unauthorised access to regulated or dangerous substances in violation of applicable laws and consumer safety standards,” the ministry said.

item.title: Apple India’s FY26 Profit Jumps 66% YoY To ₹5,311 Cr, Revenue Up 31%
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Apple India reported a 66% year-on-year (YoY) increase in its net profit during the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026…
item.content:encoded:
Apple India reported a 66% year-on-year (YoY) increase in its net profit during the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26) to ₹5,311 Cr from ₹3,196 Cr it reported in the year-ago period. 

The iPhone-maker’s operating revenue increased 31.4% to ₹1.04 Lakh Cr from ₹79,060 Cr in FY25, buoyed by a significant jump in its sales of iPhone, MacBooks, iPad and other products. 

Apple India’s revenue from the sale of traded goods jumped to ₹99,068 Cr in the period under review, an almost 33% increase from ₹74,680 Cr in FY25. 

Its remaining operating revenue came from its support services, including Apple Care services, which grew 7.6% YoY to 4,292.8 Cr, while revenue from maintenance contracts fetched ₹492.4 Cr. 

Meanwhile, it earned ₹463 Cr from finance income and ₹291 Cr in other income during the fiscal year, taking its total income to ₹1.05 Cr. 

To note, the tech giant had earlier said that its India market operations delivered strong double-digit revenue growth during the June quarter (Q1 FY27), aided by exceptional demand for its more affordable MacBook Neo. 

Apple has continued to deepen its presence in India, expanding beyond its flagship iPhone business into a broader ecosystem spanning Macs, iPads, wearables and services. India has also become central to Apple’s global manufacturing strategy, with the country emerging as one of Apple’s largest production bases outside China. iPhone exports from India crossed ₹2 Lakh Cr in FY26.

It is now expanding its foothold in the country further through its financial services unit Apple Pay, which it launched in India last month in partnership with Axis Bank. The rollout has allowed iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch users to make payments in apps, online and at contactless-enabled stores, with Mac support coming soon.

It has already onboarded a host of merchants for Apple Pay, including Apple Store physical locations, Blinkit, Chaayos, Comet, Croma, Interflora, ixigo, Le15 Patisserie, Reliance brands, Tata 1mg, Zomato, among others.

Despite the strong growth, the company now expects supply constraints in the coming months due to a shortfall in advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity, along with constraints around memory components. The company expects the constraints to affect availability of iPhones, Macs and iPads globally, which could also have an impact on markets such as India if component shortages persist.

Where Did Apple India Spend In FY26? 

Apple India’s total expenses during the fiscal year under review grew 28% to ₹96,224 Cr from ₹75,190.7 Cr it reported in FY25. Notably, the company paid ₹10,373.7 Cr in license fee during the year, more than double of ₹4,257.8 Cr it spent in FY25.

Purchase Of Traded Goods: Apple India’s inventory expenses stood at ₹78,228.7 Cr during the fiscal year, a 21.6% jump from ₹64,335.8 Cr in FY25, making it the company’s biggest expense. 

Employee Benefit Expenses: Its expenditure under this head surged 13% YoY to ₹3,531.3 from ₹3,126.1 Cr in FY25, including spending on wages, PF contributions, gratuity and staff welfare. Notably, the company paid ₹17,80.4 Cr in salaries and bonuses during the year. 

Marketing & Advertisement: Another major expense head, marketing and advertising cost Apple India ₹1,075.2 Cr during the year, increasing 22.6% YoY from ₹877.1 Cr in the year-ago period.

item.title: IndiQube To Invest ₹35 Cr In Office Space Developer SaiEdge Realty
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Listed coworking space provider IndiQube Spaces’ board has approved an investment of up to ₹35 Cr in SaiEdge Realty to…
item.content:encoded:
Listed coworking space provider IndiQube Spaces’ board has approved an investment of up to ₹35 Cr in SaiEdge Realty to acquire up to a 49% stake.

SaiEdge will develop commercial office spaces that IndiQube intends to lease upon completion, the latter said in an exchange filing 

The investment will be made in cash, in one or more tranches, through subscriptions to equity shares and/or convertible securities.

Incorporated on July 28, SaiEdge has a paid-up share capital of ₹1 Lakh and is yet to commence operations or generate turnover. Its remaining shareholding will be held by other investors.

Separately, IndiQube’s board appointed Ishwar Subramanian as an additional independent director, effective yesterday. His appointment for a five-year term, ending October 18, 2031, is subject to shareholder approval.

The board also reconstituted the company’s audit committee, with Subramanian appointed as chairperson. Independent director Sachi Krishana and executive director and CEO Rishi Das will serve as members.

The appointment follows the resignation of independent director Avalur Gopalaratnam Muralikrishnan, effective yesterday. 

Founded in 2015 by Rishi Das and Meghna Agarwal, Bengaluru-based IndiQube provides managed workspaces to startups, SMEs, and large enterprises. Its offering covers workspace design, interior fit-outs, facilities management, and employee services such as transport. 

The company primarily leases properties and customises them to suit clients’ requirements. It competes with Awfis and Smartworks, among other flexible workspace operators, with its model centred on tailored offices and long-term client relationships. 

IndiQube listed on the bourses in July 2025, following a ₹700 Cr IPO comprising a ₹650 Cr fresh issue and a ₹50 Cr OFS by its cofounders. Its shares debuted at ₹218.70 on the BSE and ₹216 on the NSE, discounts of 7.7% and 8.8%, respectively, to the ₹237 issue price.

On the financial front, IndiQube’s net loss narrowed 35% to ₹23.9 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹36.8 Cr a year earlier. However, loss widened 5% QoQ from ₹22.7 Cr.

Operating revenue grew 37% YoY and 5% QoQ to ₹422.6 Cr. Including other income of ₹26.1 Cr, total income stood at ₹448.7 Cr. The company is yet to report its Q2 FY27 numbers.

item.title: Founder Salaries Tracker FY26: How Much Did India’s Startup Founders Earn?
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Twenty-two founders across 15 new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹61.28 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 4.6% from…
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-two founders across 15 new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹61.28 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 4.6% from ₹58.54 Cr in FY25, according to data compiled by Inc42. Average fixed remuneration per founder increased to ₹2.79 Cr from ₹2.66 Cr.

Of these, 16 founders received increases in fixed pay, four saw reductions, and two reported unchanged remuneration.

Honasa Consumer cofounder Ghazal Alagh recorded the highest percentage increase, with her fixed remuneration rising 60% to ₹2.4 Cr from ₹1.5 Cr. Delhivery cofounder Sahil Barua followed with a 21.4% increase to ₹3.4 Cr from ₹2.8 Cr.

Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal recorded the steepest percentage decline, with his remuneration falling 34.8% to ₹4.5 Cr from ₹6.9 Cr. Nykaa founder Falguni Nayar’s fixed pay fell 14% to ₹74 Lakh from ₹86 Lakh, while Swiggy cofounder Sriharsha Majety’s remuneration declined 12.5% to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr.

Lenskart cofounder Peyush Bansal drew the highest fixed remuneration among the founders tracked, despite a 1.7% decline to ₹5.7 Cr from ₹5.8 Cr. Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar followed with ₹4.8 Cr each, ahead of Ola Electric’s Aggarwal at ₹4.5 Cr and Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma at ₹4 Cr. Sharma’s fixed remuneration remained unchanged from FY25.

However, fixed pay tells only part of the story. Peyush Bansal received ₹12 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives – more than twice his fixed remuneration – along with perquisites and retirement benefits. Fellow Lenskart cofounder Neha Bansal received ₹6 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives, in addition to her ₹2.7 Cr fixed pay.
Honasa Consumer cofounder Varun Alagh received ₹2.4 Cr in performance incentives, equal to his fixed remuneration.

Share-based compensation also featured prominently. Majety’s ESOP gains stood at ₹549.3 Cr, while Delhivery cofounder Kapil Bharati recorded ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains.

Separately, the cost of stock options granted to FirstCry founder Supam Maheshwari stood at ₹31.7 Cr. He also received ₹2.1 Cr in perquisites and ₹84 Lakh in performance incentives.

These components require separate treatment. Stock-option costs and ESOP-related benefits do not necessarily represent cash received by a founder during the year and should be distinguished from fixed salaries and cash incentives.

Peyush Bansal | Lenskart 

The Lenskart cofounder and CEO earned ₹5.7 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26. In addition to his fixed pay, Bansal also received ₹12 Cr in bonus and performance incentives, along with ₹24.04 Lakh in perquisites and ₹7.5 Lakh in retirals.

Lenskart’s net profit rose 69% YoY to ₹500.9 Cr in FY26, while operating revenue increased 33% YoY to ₹8,814 Cr. Its profit growth was aided by operating leverage, premiumisation, and growth in international markets.

Vidit Aatrey & Sanjeev Kumar | Meesho

Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar each earned ₹4.8 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 6.7% from ₹4.5 Cr a year earlier.

The data reviewed by Inc42 did not disclose additional perks for either founder.

The ecommerce company’s operating revenue increased 34.5% YoY to ₹12,626 Cr in FY26, while its net loss narrowed 65.6% YoY to ₹1,357.7 Cr.

Its annual transacting user base grew 33% YoY to 26.4 Cr in Q4 FY26, while order volumes increased 43% YoY to 71.7 Cr during the quarter.

Bhavish Aggarwal | Ola Electric 

Ola Electric founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal earned ₹4.5 Cr in remuneration in FY26, compared with ₹6.9 Cr in FY25. 

In FY26, the EV maker’s net loss narrowed nearly 20% to ₹1,833 Cr from ₹2,276 Cr in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue nearly halved to ₹2,460 Cr from ₹4,932 Cr.

Bhanu Chopra | RateGain 

RateGain founder and CEO Bhanu Chopra earned ₹3.7 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, unchanged from FY25.

The company’s operating revenue rose 69.4% to ₹1,823.6 Cr from ₹1,076.7 Cr, while net profit declined 6.9% to ₹194.4 Cr from ₹208.9 Cr.

Sahil Barua & Kapil Bharati | Delhivery 

Delhivery cofounders Sahil Barua and Kapil Bharati earned ₹3.4 Cr and ₹3.3 Cr, respectively, in fixed remuneration in FY26.

Barua’s fixed pay increased 21.4% from ₹2.8 Cr in FY25, while Bharati’s rose 17.9% from ₹2.8 Cr.

In addition, Barua received ₹33.7 Lakh in performance incentives. Bharati received ₹33 Lakh in performance incentives and ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains.

The logistics company’s operating revenue rose 17% YoY to ₹10,486 Cr in FY26, while net profit grew 8% YoY to ₹321 Cr.

Vijay Shekhar Sharma | Paytm 

Paytm founder and CEO Vijay Shekhar Sharma earned ₹4 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, unchanged from the previous year. He also received ₹33 Lakh in perquisites.

The fintech company reported its first full-year net profit of ₹552 Cr in FY26, compared with a loss of ₹663 Cr in FY25.

Operating revenue increased 22.3% YoY to ₹8,437 Cr. It also posted an EBITDA of ₹502 Cr, against an EBITDA loss of ₹1,506 Cr in the previous year.

Tarun Mehta & Swapnil Jain | Ather

Ather Energy cofounders Tarun Mehta and Swapnil Jain each earned ₹2.1 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 5% from ₹2 Cr a year earlier. They also received ₹90 Lakh each in variable compensation, taking their individual fixed and variable pay to ₹3 Cr.

The EV maker’s operating revenue rose 62.8% YoY to ₹3,671.8 Cr, while its net loss narrowed 36.3% YoY to ₹517.2 Cr.

EBITDA loss declined 51.6% YoY to ₹257 Cr, with its EBITDA margin improving to -6.7% from -23% in FY25.
